topic: Love bombing: what research actually says
title: Love Bombing: What Research Actually Says
voiceover: What does research actually say about love bombing? In 2017, Strutzenberg and colleagues published what they described as the first study to empirically examine love-bombing. They defined it as excessive communication early in a romantic relationship, used to gain power and control. They surveyed 484 college students at a large southern university. Love-bombing was linked to narcissistic tendencies and insecure attachment. It was also linked to lower self-esteem. And it was associated with more text and media use in relationships. The study was a survey of college students, so it can't show cause and effect. That makes it early research, not a settled diagnosis. So treat 'love bombing' as a description of a pattern in one study, and not as a test for who someone is. Tomorrow: where does the word gaslighting come from?

description: What does research say about love bombing? A 2017 survey of 484 college students linked it with narcissistic tendencies, insecure attachment and lower self-esteem, but it is early, correlational research. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Strutzenberg, C. C., Wiersma-Mosley, J. D., Jozkowski, K. N., & Becnel, J. N. (2017). Love-bombing: A narcissistic approach to relationship formation. Discovery, The Student Journal of Dale Bumpers College, 18(1) (University of Arkansas).
accuracy_note: SENSITIVE / EARLY RESEARCH. One survey study (Strutzenberg et al. 2017; college students; correlational). The video does not diagnose anyone or claim causes, and does not call love bombing a clinical diagnosis. Educational, not therapy or medical advice.
